Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In Britain's peerage system, do Dukes outrank Earls or are they equal?
Answer: According to the definitive Debrett’s Guide to the Ranks and Privileges of the Peerage (often just called Debrett’s), the five degrees of the peerage, in descending order of precedence, are: Duke/Duchess, Marquess/Marchioness, Earl/Countess, Viscount/Viscountess, and Baron/Baroness. This obviously excludes the members of the Royal Family itself, which has its own quite complicated orders of precedence. There are also Royal Dukes, such as the Duke of Edinburgh who are entitled to the title of Prince and, indeed, Royal Earls, who outrank ordinary Earls. For instance the Earl of Wessex is Prince Edward, who is also now the Duke of Edinburgh, the Earl of Forfar, and Viscount Severn. Within their rank, precedence generally conforms to the age of the title. I believe that the oldest extant English Peerage is the Earldom of Arundel (created in 1138) which is held by the Duke of Norfolk and used by his heir as a courtesy title. Arundel Castle - worth visiting, nice gardens - you can see the original motte (dating from 1067) in the middle There are obviously lots of variations catering for the differences between English and Scottish peers, hereditary and life peers, office holders (e.g. Lord Chancellor), bishops, the various orders of knighthood, etc., etc. It may surprise some non-natives to learn that 99.9% of British people go through their whole lives without the slightest idea about any of this as it doesn’t impinge on daily life in any way. I live in Sussex, but I am in no way beholden to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, although I’d probably be polite if introduced to them - but then I’m polite when introduced to anybody.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was an invasion of Britain through Pas-de-Calais considered easier than the invasion at Normandy?
Answer: Not at all. No seaborne invasion should be considered easy, but the planned German invasion of the United Kingdom, Operation Seelöwe or Sealion, would have been an extremely risky, practically suicidal venture. If we are talking about the fact that it is a shorter distance across the Channel from the Pas-de-Calais rather than to the Baie de la Seine (Normandy) then it needs to be noted that Seelöwe landing beaches extended from Ramsgate to Portsmouth, a broad frontage at least three times wider than that of the Allies in Normandy and involving both long and short transits. There is no particular advantage in distance. Hitler laid down the following conditions for launching Seelöwe: (1) that the Germans had gained air superiority, (2) that all British minefields were swept and the invasion beaches isolated, (3) that the Royal Navy be unable to intervene. The fact that none of these conditions, which all presupposed victory in the Battle of Britain, were met meant that the operation was stillborn. However, even had they been met, Operation Seelöwe would still have been impossible to execute successfully. Planning for Seelöwe was shoehorned into less than two months, whilst the detailed planning for D-Day took more than a year. The Allies had a vast fleet of some 7,000 specially designed ships and landing craft of various types, whilst the Germans relied mainly on 2,400 river barges most of which were unpowered, were totally unsuitable for crossing the Channel in any kind of rough sea, and were very slow and lacking any kind of defences. German invasion fleet Allied invasion fleet Furthermore, the Germans had no capability whatsoever to supply their invasion force with logistical backup, whilst the Allies had prepared the Mulberry floating harbours, the Pluto (Pipe Line Under The Ocean) fuel pipeline, DUKW amphibious trucks and a huge logistical support operation. There is really no comparison between the two operations. Operation Seelöwe was the very definition of wing-and-a-prayer, whilst Operation Neptune, the naval part of Overlord, was meticulously planned and prepared for.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If German tanks had been sent to Omaha Beach on D-Day, could they have stopped the Allied invasion?
Answer: No, because Omaha Beach was only one of five beaches stormed on D-Day. Failure on Omaha would have been a significant setback, but it wouldn’t have stopped the whole Allied invasion. Also no, because there were no significant armoured forces within reach that could have been sent to Omaha Beach on D-Day. The divisions that were holding the coast were mostly static infantry divisions and thought themselves lucky if they had a company of assault guns assigned. Whilst Army Group B, consisting of the 7th and 15th Armies, holding the Channel Coast from Amsterdam to Lorient was under the command of von Rundstedt, the Panzer divisions were initially formed in Panzer Group West, under the command of von Schweppenburg. These nine divisions (2nd, 21st, 116th, 1st SS, 12th SS, 17th SS, 2nd SS, 9th and 11th) were tasked with covering the entire coastline of France, Holland, and Belgium, including the Mediterranean coast of France. The Germans decided to hold their main armoured units in reserve and at some distance from the coast so that they could react to wherever the invasion occurred. Their plan called for a mobile defence in depth to hold the allied invaders in check until a mobile strategic reserve could be brought to bear for a decisive counterattack and a battle of annihilation. Bearing in mind that the most likely invasion site was still thought to be the Pas de Calais rather than Normandy, the disposition of the Panzer divisions on June 6th 1944 was as follows: 2nd SS and 9th were on the Mediterranean coast, 11th Panzer was on the Atlantic coast, and 1st SS and 2nd were covering northern France and the Low Countries. That leaves a central group consisting of 116th, Pz Lehr, 12th SS and 21st roughly centred to the west of Paris and about 90 miles from the Normandy beaches. Rommel wanted to position the Panzer divisions nearer the coast where they could react more quickly but his views were opposed by von Rundstedt, von Schweppenburg, and Guderian. In reality, the Germans were in an impossible position. Stationing the Panzers nearer the coast would have allowed them to react more quickly, but it would also have put them directly under the guns of the immensely powerful Allied naval task forces stationed off the beaches. They would have entered the fight with less attrition, but would then have been rendered combat ineffective very quickly by Allied air and sea-power. Rommel had wanted to position 12th SS Panzer in the vicinity of Isigny, which would have put it around 12 miles from Omaha Beach rather than more than 100 miles to the east near Evreux. If 12th SS had indeed been stationed at Isigny, it would very probably have had a significant impact on the landings at Omaha Beach as it could have intervened before the Allies had managed to land much armour of their own, and it might possibly have caused the landings on Omaha to fail. Panzerkampfwagen IV Ausf H of 12. SS-Panzer-Division In fact, the nearest Panzer division to the US beaches was 21st Panzer, which was initially positioned near Falaise about 45 miles from Omaha Beach. In the event 21st Panzer was the only German panzer division to play a part on D-Day when it attempted to drive between the British and Canadian beaches in the vicinity of Caen. Whilst one kampfgruppe did succeed in reaching the coast at Lion sur Mer, their position was clearly untenable and they were forced to withdraw north of Caen, losing significant numbers of armoured vehicles in the process.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If the British Army was attacked by Russia, could they defeat them without assistance from other countries such as France or America?
Answer: The simple answer is no, and it has never been intended that it should do so - hence NATO. The only countries that could withstand a conventional attack by Russia on their own are the United States, China, and possibly India and Turkey. Countries with large populations and considerable military resources. [Edit: I’m getting a lot of repetitive comments. This question is clearly a thought or Gedanken experiment rather than a probable scenario. It does not postulate an invasion of the UK, and any such question would require a lot more information about how we came to that pass. Below, I simply give a comparison of the two forces in a conflict where we are defending (say) the Baltic States - where we currently have a trip-wire battalion stationed.] In raw terms Russia has twice the population of the United Kingdom and although the UK has a larger economy than Russia in dollar terms, it is smaller when compared in PPP terms. Manpower is a major factor in armies and Russia can recruit men far more cheaply that the United Kingdom. The fact is that the average salary in Russia is certainly less than half of that in the UK and probably under a third. With regard to what the two countries spend on defence and the size of their forces, there is no comparison. I believe that Russia is spending about 6% of it GDP on defence whilst the UK is spending 2% - and some of that appears to be the result of creative accounting. The Russian Army has over 3,000,000 men (including paramilitary forces) whilst the United Kingdom has around 250,000 (in all three services), and that number is shrinking quite fast. British Army - a shrinking resource The quality of our men and our equipment is almost certainly superior to that of the Russians on a one-to-one basis, but this can only get you so far. It is a dangerous position to assume that a few high quality, but fragile, platforms will win the day over a significantly larger mass of average equipment. There is also the matter of logistics and most sources seem to agree that the United Kingdom only has the logistics to fight for around two weeks before its war stocks would be exhausted. At that point, its choices would be to surrender or to go nuclear. Effectively, our conventional forces have, for decades, been nothing more than a trip-wire, a small breathing space for diplomacy, before we have to escalate to the use of nuclear weapons. Of course, if we are discussing an attack on the British Isles, the Russians would have to get here which would be a significant problem for them. Then the probabilities depend on whether the Russians have advanced to the Channel Coast or not. We’d need a significantly more detailed scenario to be able to comment on that, and so I am assuming that we are discussing British forces fighting on the Continent - in defence of the Baltic States for instance.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is Gold “Au” and Silver “Ag” while other elements are named after their names?
Answer: Elements named after the turn of the 19th Century have symbols (abbreviations) that reflect their names (e.g. Cf for Californium) but some elements, named prior to 1810 have symbols that do not match their (English) names, the most recent being Potassium (K) named in 1807. There are eleven symbols that don’t match the element’s modern name. Those are subtle reminders of the history of alchemy and chemistry and the process of the discovery of elements over the millennia. Eight of these elements were recognized by the ancient Greeks and Romans, and the abbreviations for those are based on a Latin or Greek term for the element. Therefore, gold is Au (aurum in Latin), silver is Ag (argentum in Latin), copper is Cu (cuprum in Latin), iron is Fe (ferrum in Latin), tin is Sn (stannum in Latin), lead is Pb (plumbum in Latin), antomony is Sb (stibium in Latin), and mercury is Hg (hydrargyrum in Greek). Roman gold and silver coins Tin (Sn) is interesting because the Romans called it plumbum candidum, or white lead and stannum meant an alloy of silver and lead - coming to mean tin in the fourth century. In French, tin is étain, in Spanish estaño, in Italian stagno, in Irish stán and in English the old name is remembered in the Stannary towns such as Truro and Tavistock where tin smelted in the area was assessed and coined. Potassium (K) was identified during the Middle Ages, but was named by Humphrey Davy who first isolated the pure element, K stands for kalium, a medieval Latin term for potash (from the root word alkali, which in turn comes from Arabic al-qalyah or plant ashes), tungsten is W because it was first identified in 1780 within the mineral known as wolframite by French scientist Antoine Lavoisier, and sodium is Na because it was first isolated by Humphry Davy (again) in 1807 and he was referring to natron, an Arabic word for the salt used by the Egyptians to mummify people. In fact, Davy is isolated, by using electrolysis, many elements for the first time: potassium (K) and sodium (Na) in 1807, and calcium (Ca), strontium (Sr), barium (Ba), and magnesium (Mg) in 1808 but, in these latter cases he followed the more modern naming convention.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is the 1917 mutiny at etaples during WW1 not widely taught in UK schools whereas the French military mutiny during WWI is taught?
Answer: Because the aren’t comparable in any meaningful way. The Étaples mutiny occurred out of the line at the Base Depot at Étaples and resulted from the unnecessarily harsh regime in the camp. It lasted for four days and was more of a riot than a mutiny. One man, William Wood, was shot by a military policeman during the rioting and one, Jesse Short, was tried for Mutinous Conduct and executed by firing squad. Three men received prison sentences of ten years and another forty-three received field punishment or short prison sentences. British soldiers training at Étaples The French Army mutinies of 1917 were a different kettle of fish altogether. They involved forty-nine divisions to one extent or another, nearly half of the French divisions on the Western Front, and lasted for six weeks with the men involved refusing all orders to attack and 27,000 men deserting. As a result, 629 mutineers were sentenced to death. Most of these sentences were commuted, but forty-nine men were executed by firing-squad.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What date did the WWI conscription end in the UK?
Answer: It was surprisingly difficult to locate an answer to this one as some sources say 1919 and some 1920. The correct answer is that conscription in the UK, under the terms of the Military Service Act of 1916 and its Amendments, ended on the 31st of March, 1920. Conscription was never applied to Ireland. Conscription was introduced in January 1916 targeting single men aged 18 to 41. The scope was expanded to include married men in May 1916, and in late 1918 the upper age limit was extended to 51 - with a provision to extend it to 56. Some 4.9 million men were enlisted in the British army between 1914 and 1918. Of these 2.4 million enlisted prior to the introduction of conscription and 2.5 million after the introduction of conscription. However, it has been suggested that only 1.3 million men were actually conscripted. The man responsible for announcing the end of conscription was one W.S. Churchill, then Secretary of State for War and Air. His speech to the House of Commons is worth reading: On the 31st of next month conscription will be abolished, and within a month from that date the last conscript is entitled to be released from; the Army. The vast process of demobilisation will then be completed. In the interval, and only just in time, we have succeeded in raising and organising, unit by unit, an entirely new Volunteer Army, which by the time conscription lapses will, we estimate, number about 220,000 men, exclusive of those serving in India… In other words, we have recruited in a single year what is, broadly speaking, the pre-war Regular Army, and we have organised the additional troops which are needed to discharge our temporary and new liabilities. I venture to think that that is a remarkable achievement… I will invite the Committee to consider what sort of language would have been used supposing we had not succeeded, and supposing I had had to stand here to-day, as I might easily have done, and point out that, owing to the fact that we had not been able to recruit a volunteer army, I must ask for a prolongation of compulsory military service, keeping at any rate the younger conscripts who took no part in the War for another year to come. We have abolished conscription. At the General Election we pledged ourselves to fight for the abolition of conscription at the Peace Conference, but we were very careful to add that our own action must depend on what others did. Our representatives fought at the Peace Conference for the abolition of conscription, but they fought with singularly little success. In fact, there was no response at all to the representations which they made. The only other great nation whom we have succeeded in persuading to abolish conscription is Germany, and that is only under dire compulsion and as part of her punishment for having lost the War. The following States, among others—I do not pretend for a moment that my list is exhaustive—retain compulsory service as the basis of their military system, and apparently have no intention of departing from it: France, Italy, Japan, Spain, Portugal, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Holland, Denmark. Rumania, Greece, Poland, Jugo-Slavia, Czecho-Slovakia, the United States, the originator of the League of Nations, Russia—here we tread on controversial ground—the home of advanced political thought, where there is not only military conscription but industrial conscription also. Undiscouraged and undeterred by our failure to convert others, we have proceeded to set an example ourselves. Alone among the nations we have decided to abolish compulsory military service, and I venture to think that this action, coming as it does apart from the action of all other nations, deserves additional recognition from those who have so vehemently demanded it. We alone, who have far greater extent of territory to control, who are responsible for a far larger mass of human beings in every part of the world, have returned to that voluntary system which we pursued before the War. At the Armistice we had on the whole the strongest army in the world. Our normal army and our present army will be weaker than the army of Belgium. And then we are called militarists. Alone among the nations we have abandoned compulsory service. Yet I suppose we shall be treated to a continuance of the line of criticism which brands us as a Jingo Government and accuses the Secretary of State for War as being a bellicose and ambitious administrator. House of Commons, Monday the 23rd February 1920

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If Nazi Germany had won the Battle of Britain, would the Royal Navy have tried to interfere with the Operation Sea Lion landings?
Answer: They certainly would have. Apart from some curious off-the-wall operations such as Operation Lucid, the Royal Navy’s anti-invasion preparations were fairly standard, with ships covering both the East coast and the Channel. The Home Fleet was stationed far to the North at Scapa Flow in the Orkneys where it could cover the North Atlantic, Norwegian Sea, and North Sea. It would have taken over twenty-four hours for the Home Fleet to intervene in the Channel, but the Home Fleet was not the only force at hand. At the outbreak of war, the Royal Navy had nine battleships, four aircraft carriers, seventeen cruisers, and ninety-six destroyers in Home Waters. Seven battleships (including Hood), an aircraft carrier, twelve cruisers, and seventeen destroyers were with the Home Fleet at Scapa Flow. The rest of the force was split between Rosyth, Humber, Portland, Dover, Portsmouth and Plymouth . Royal Navy Destroyers at sea By September 1940, there were twelve destroyers and one cruiser were based on the Tyne with the aircraft carrier Argus. Ten destroyers were based at Dover and Portsmouth, a cruiser and three destroyers at Sheerness, three cruisers and seven destroyers at the Humber, nine destroyers at Harwich, and two cruisers at Rosyth. The battleships Rodney, Nelson, and Hood, three cruisers and a destroyer flotilla were moved south to Rosyth and the Revenge was moved to Plymouth. By early September the Royal Navy had between Plymouth and Harwich, 4 light cruisers and 57 destroyers together with around fifty MTBs. Together with the Home Fleet, this was far more naval power than the Germans could possibly commit to any invasion even if they wanted to risk their heavy units. However, in all likelihood, any invasion would have been faced by light units: cruisers, destroyers, motor torpedo boats, and submarines. The invasion areas were simply too constricted and too vulnerable to air power to deploy heavy units, except in extremis. In the famous Operation Sea Lion wargame conducted by the Royal Military Academy (Sandhurst) in 1974, the heavy units of the Home Fleet were ordered to stand by but not actually used. If you are wondering why I am discussing the outcome of this wargame, it is because it is the largest simulation of Sea Lion ever conducted. The scenario was based on the known plans of each side and Admiralty weather records for September 1940. The umpire for the Kriegsmarine was Vizeadmiral Friederich Ruge who commanded the naval escort and support operations for the invasion of Poland and then FdM West (part of the North Sea and Channel operations) from 1940 to 1943. Someone who should know what he was talking about. The following extract covers the naval battles but omit the Heer and Luftwaffe elements. It should be noted that many of the Royal Navy’s losses described below would have been inflicted by the Luftwaffe. 22nd September The first wave hit the beaches at dawn. Elements of 9 divisions were landed between Folkestone and Rottingdean (near Brighton). In addition 7th FJ (parachute) Div landed at Lympne to take the airfield. The invasion fleet suffered minor losses from MTBs (motor torpedo boats) during the night crossing, but the Royal Navy lost one CA (cruiser) and three DDs (destroyers) sunk, with one CA and two DDs damaged, whilst sinking three German DDs. 22nd - 23rd September The U-Boats, Luftwaffe and few surface ships had lost contact with the Royal Navy, but then a cruiser squadron with supporting DDs entered the Channel narrows and had to run the gauntlet of long range coastal guns, E-Boats, and Stukas. Two CAs were sunk and one damaged. A diversionary German naval sortie from Norway was completely destroyed. Sorties by MTBs and DDs inflicted losses on German shipping in the Channel. German shipping losses on the first day amounted to over 25% of their invasion fleet. 23rd Sept 1400 - 1900 hrs The Home Fleet had pulled out of air range however, leaving the fight in the hands of 57 DDs and 17 CAs plus a number of MTBs. The Germans could put very little surface strength against this. Waves of DDs and CAs entered the Channel, and although two were sunk by U-Boats, they sank one U-Boat in return and did not stop. The German flotilla at Le Havre put to sea (3 DDs, 14 E-Boats) and at dusk intercepted the British, but were wiped out, losing all three DDs and 7 E-Boats. Sep 24th dawn - Sep 28th The German second echelon set sail, the weather calmed, and U-Boats, E-Boats and fighters covered them. However at daylight 5th destroyer flotilla found the barges still ten miles off the coast and tore them to shreds. The Germans disabled two CAs and four DDs, but 65% of the barges were sunk. Lacking supplies and reinforcements the Germans conducted a hasty evacuation. Of the 90,000 troops who landed on 22nd September, only 15,400 returned to France, the rest were killed or captured.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In "Masters of the Air", they claim the USAF did precision bombing by day and the RAF did area bombing by night. Is that true? Didn't the RAF sometimes bomb by day?
Answer: There are actually two different questions being asked here, one about day vs night bombing and one about precision vs area bombing. In the 1920’s the theories of Giulio Douhet were much in favour and his book Il dominio dell'aria (The Command of the Air) was very widely read. Although experience proved Douhet’s theories to be wide of the mark, he had a significant influence over military and political thinking in the pre-war period. In the 1930s, there was a brief period where multi-engine aircraft (bombers) were faster than single-engine aircraft (fighters) and in 1932, this led to Stanley Baldwin giving a speech in Parliament in which he concluded that the bomber will always get through: I think it is well also for the man in the street to realize that there is no power on earth that can protect him from being bombed, whatever people may tell him. The bomber will always get through, and it is very easy to understand that if you realise the area of space. Take any large town you like on this island or on the Continent within reach of an aerodrome. For the defence of that town and its suburbs you have to split up the air into sectors for defence. Calculate that the bombing aeroplanes will be at least 20,000ft. high in the air, and perhaps higher, and it is a matter of mathematical calculation that you will have sectors of from ten to hundreds of cubic miles. Imagine one hundred cubic miles covered with cloud and fog, and you can calculate how many aeroplanes you would have to throw into that to have much chance of catching odd aeroplanes as they fly through it. It cannot be done, and there is no expert in Europe who will say that it can. The only defence is in offence, which means that you have got to kill more women and children more quickly than the enemy if you want to save yourselves. I mention that so that people may realise what is waiting for them when the next war comes. However, technology, including the introduction of radar, marched on and by the time that WW2 broke out the fighters once again had the upper hand. In 1940, the Germans and then the British quickly found that bomber attacks made in daylight resulted in catastrophic losses, a lesson painfully relearned by the USAAF in 1943. As a result, both sides switched to bombing at night. RAF Lancaster over Hamburg However, it would be incorrect to say that the British never bombed during the day, although the vast majority of sorties were certainly made at night. From 1942 onwards, the RAF conducted daylight operations as deemed necessary and, obviously the tempo of daylight operations picked up markedly after D-Day as the Luftwaffe disintegrated and the Allies gained control of the air over Germany. For example: on 27 August 1944, against the Rheinpreussen synthetic oil refinery at Homberg/Meerbeck. Cloud cover over the target was 7/10ths and the attack took place using the same Oboe marking techniques and green target indicators used in night raids… although flak had been reported as “heavy” over the target, no bombers were shot down and the escorting squadrons of Spitfires drove off the Luftwaffe. Some of these daylight raids were of significant size: On 3 September 1944, 675 aircraft participated in daylight raids against six German airfields in Holland, targeting runways and hangars. Only one Halifax bomber was lost to flak over Venlo. RAF Lancasters bomb through cloud during a daylight raid in the summer of 1944 When the USAAF started mounting deep-penetration daylight raids they found, in turn, that their losses were unsustainable. Eighth Air Force losses were so heavy that, statistically, USAAF bomber crews had no chance of surviving a tour. In the first Schweinfurt-Regensburg raid, 60 bombers were lost, and many more damaged beyond repair, out of the 376 participating (16%). After a two month pause to regroup, another deep raid was made on Schweinfurt, this time suffering 77 losses (26%). The shocking scale of these losses led to a four month pause in deep-penetration raids at the end of 1943. Despite the heavy armament of the bombers it was clear that USAAF’s pre-war doctrine of the self-defending bomber formations was deficient and that long-range fighter escort was an essential requirement for deep-penetration daylight raids. USAAF B-17 combat box It is also worth noting in passing that whilst the USAAF bombers claimed 288 German fighters on the first raid, Luftwaffe records show that only 26 were actually downed. That’s a real exchange rate of one fighter downed for every 2.3 bombers lost, rather than the claimed rate of 4.8 fighters downed for every bomber lost. In other words, a 23:1 ratio of crew losses, which is clearly not sustainable. During the pause the Eighth Air Force worked with RAF Bomber Command to experiment with night bombing and flew several missions to see if it was possible to transfer to night bombing. After eight missions, it was determined the B-17s needed further modifications and that the USAAF crews required considerable additional training to perform night bombing raids. The deus-ex-machina event that saved the USAAF’s daylight strategic bombing campaign from disaster was the timely arrival of the new escort fighters. The first P-51 Mustang unit arrived in December 1943, and although the P-38 proved unsuitable for use in Europe, the P-47D also proved its worth as a medium and, later, long-range escort in the late war. The answer to the first part of this question is therefore that the RAF mostly bombed at night because the technology for effective long-range escort fighters did not exist for the first four years of the war and this made daylight raids prohibitively expensive. Conversely, the USAAF was able to bomb by day in the last eighteen months of the war because of the arrival of long-range escort fighters. As to the question of accuracy, I have no interest in discussing the moral issues involved in area bombing, although I am sure that people will emote in the comments in the usual wildly unbalanced way. What I will discuss is whether there was any such thing as precision bombing in today’s commonly accepted sense. We do not regard a fifteen-foot square as being difficult to hit from an altitude of 30,000 feet, provided the new Army M-4 bombsight, together with the Stabilized Bombing Approach Equipment is used. Theodore Barth, Norden In reality, despite the hype, the famous Norden bombsight offered no significant advantages over the British SABS or German Lotfernrohr 7 sights, and, in the event, it turned out that what was possible in ideal conditions was not remotely possible in combat. A word needs to be said on the problem of accuracy in attack. Before the war, the U .S. Army Air Forces had advanced bombing techniques to their highest level of development and had trained a limited number of crews to a high degree of precision in bombing under target range conditions, thus leading to the expressions "pin point" and "pickle barrel" bombing . However, it was not possible to approach such standards of accuracy under battle conditions imposed over Europe . Many limiting factors intervened ; target obscuration by clouds, fog, smoke screens and industrial haze; enemy fighter opposition which necessitated defensive bombing formations, thus restricting freedom of maneuver; antiaircraft artillery defenses, demanding minimum time exposure of the attacking force in order to keep losses down ; and finally, time limitations imposed on combat crew training after the war began . It was considered that enemy opposition made formation flying and formation attack a necessary tactical and technical procedure . Bombing patterns resulted-only a portion of which could fall on small precision targets . The rest spilled over on adjacent plants, or built-up areas, or in open fields… Unfortunately, the major portion of bombing operations over Germany had to be conducted under weather and battle conditions that restricted bombing technique, and accuracy suffered accordingly . Conventionally the air forces designated as "the target area" a circle having a radius of 1000 feet around the aiming point of attack . While accuracy improved during the war, Survey studies show that, in the over-all, only about 20% of the bombs aimed at precision targets fell within this target area. THE UNITED STATES STRATEGIC BOMBING SURVEY USAAF bombers operated in combat boxes sometimes up to a kilometre across and two kilometres deep and dropped their bombs on the command of a lead bomber - who was the only one equipped with a Norden bombsight. It is clear that this practice could not lead to precision bombing as we think of it today. One analysis states that 648 bombs were required to guarantee a 96% chance of two hits on a 400 x 500 ft target, but the other 646 bombs also went somewhere. Precision bombing was emphasised as a sop to US public opinion (except in the case of Japan where it apparently wasn’t an issue). It must always be borne in mind that the bomber war was characterised by the tremendous pace of technological development as measure and countermeasure followed each other with bewildering rapidity. What was possible in 1944 wasn’t remotely feasible in 1940 and this makes a huge difference in the way that the RAF and USAAF strategic bombing campaigns evolved. For instance, throughout the course of the war the British continually invented new navigation and bombing aids such as Gee, Oboe, G-H, and the H2S centimetric ground scanning radar, as well as new tactics such as the Pathfinders, Master Bombers, and Target Indicators. Each of these advances improved accuracy significantly but genuine precision bombing remained in the realm of the low-level Mosquito light bombers, not the four-engined heavies. H2S could see through clouds and smoke screens late in the war Frankly, precision bombing was more of an aspiration than a reality as the technology to support it simply didn’t exist. In addition, the difference between bombing at night and bombing during the day in Europe, where the target was frequently obscured by clouds, fog or smokescreens, was not particularly significant. In conclusion, the RAF bombed predominantly by night between 1940 and 1943 because that was the only way to maintain an acceptable loss rate. However, by the time that the USAAF bombing campaign switched into high gear in 1944, the RAF was also transitioning to large daylight raids because the provision of long range fighter escorts made this possible. So, YES, the RAF did indeed sometimes bomb during the day and NO, the difference between RAF area attacks and USAAF precision attacks is mostly the result of unwarranted hype and the fact that the people of Great Britain, having endured the Blitz, were perhaps less squeamish about calling a spade a spade than their American cousins.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain use its own B-17 in World War II?
Answer: It’s not quite clear what the question is asking. Did Britain use the B-17 or did it have an equivalent of the B-17 four engine (heavy) bomber? The answer to both questions is in the affirmative. I think that I am correct in saying that the B-17’s very first combat mission was serving with the RAF in the summer of 1941. Twenty of the thirty eight B-17Cs produced were delivered to the RAF in the summer of 1941 where they received the British designation Fortress I and were issued to 90 Squadron, whose crews had undergone training in the United States. After the war 90 Squadron was also briefly equipped with the B-29, designated the Washington B1 by the British. B-17Cs in RAF service The B-17’s first combat mission was a high-altitude daylight raid on the naval base at Wilhelmshaven, taking place on the 8th of July 1941, and the final mission over northern Europe was flown on the 25th of September 1941 after just over two months of operations. Out of a total of fifty-one sorties, twenty-five were abandoned due to problems with the aircraft. Of the rest, fifty tons of bombs were dropped, of which about one ton hit the intended targets. Eight Fortress Is were lost for various reasons, four of them being combat related. The RAF deemed the Fortress I to be unsuitable for the type of very high-altitude operations they had envisaged as German fighters could intercept the aircraft even at its ceiling of just over 30,000ft. Coastal Command received forty-two B-17Es, designated Fortress IIA, and another nineteen long range reconnaissance B-17Fs, designated Fortress II, in 1942 for anti-submarine duties, and in February 1944, eighty-five B-17Gs, designated Fortress III, formed part of 100 (Bomber Support) Group and their aircraft were fitted with a large number of electronic countermeasures, including Airborne Cigar, to jam enemy radar sites. Coastal Command B-17 bombing up 100 Group B-17 equipped with Airborne Cigar The RAF made much more use the Consolidated B-24 Liberator four-engine bomber of which some 1,900 equipped Bomber Command in the Middle and Far-East as well as being used by Coastal Command for anti-submarine duties in the Atlantic. However, the mainstays of Bomber Command’s four engine bomber fleet were the Short Stirling (1,371 built), the Handley Page Halifax (6,178 built), and the Avro Lancaster (7,377 built). Short Stirling Handley Page Halifax Avro Lancaster There is quite a lot of national chauvinism about the relative merits of these aircraft which I’m going to attempt to avoid - as much as possible. Bomber losses are extremely difficult to quantify because there is significant sensitivity to specific conditions: period of the war, mission profile, target profile, depth of penetration, fighter support, electronic support, enemy defences, etc., etc. Therefore, averages are only, at best, indicative. I should also note that there are very many variable, and sometimes contradictory, sources out there. The B-17 suffered overall losses of around 37.5% of those built whilst the Lancaster suffered losses of around 44%. However, the Lancaster was in combat for longer and conducted more deep penetration raids. I don’t think that there is any very significant difference in loss rates if you take this into account. Typical loss rates per mission seem to have been similar: Bombing the European Axis Powers, Davis (this is for all bombers, all causes) The slightly higher loss rate of the RAF is probably simply a reflection of the higher accident rate experienced when flying at night. Overall, it appears that 40-50% of B-17 losses were due to enemy fighters and 50–60% due to flak whilst perhaps 60–70% of Lancaster losses were due to flak. This obviously reflects the fact that the RAF bombed at night. The Lancaster had a lower ceiling than the B-17 which may have given a benefit to the B-17, but with the introduction of radar-directed flak this would have diminished. The Lancaster seems to have been very slightly faster and had a rather better range. If an aircraft was shot down, B-17 crews had a slight advantage in survivability with some 40% of B-17 crew members surviving versus around 30% of Lancaster crews. However, more Lancaster crew appear to have been injured when baling out of their aircraft and, in this respect, the Lancaster seems to have been worse that both the B-17, the Halifax, and the Stirling. Of course, the loss of a B-17 caused the loss of ten crew, that of a Lancaster eight. I don’t think that there was any very significant difference in bombing accuracy, despite theoretical differences in doctrine. Most B-17s didn’t carry the Norden bombsight and bombed on command of the lead bomber. Later in the war, the development of H2S ground scanning radar and other techniques improved the bombing of both air forces at night, through overcast, and through smoke. In terms of defensive armament, I don’t think that the heavier armament of the B-17 did it much good, but its almost impossible to draw any conclusions because of the completely different doctrines employed. One factor the B-17s defensive armament was that it carried a much lighter bomb load than the Lancaster with an average of around 4,500lbs compared with 14,000lbs for the Lancaster. Obviously bomb loads varied depending on distance and target, but this is a reasonable comparison and suggests that the B-17 had to fly more sorties to drop the same weight of bombs. Had the Lancaster tried to fly daylight raids before the advent of escort fighters, it would almost certainly have suffered heavier casualties than the B-17. Having said that, the B-17 couldn’t have sustained the day offensive without escort fighters either so, effectively, there isn’t much difference. All in all, no very significant differences between the two bombers.
